rv.q: A disjointed evening begins to generate an authentic sense of the tragic.
It all plays as the best rep production you've ever seen: a mighty exercise in rhythm and diction.
This Lear feels like a dress rehearsal for Branagh – a much grander outing at some later point is surely in the works.
Peel away the brutal pruning of the text, and casting that is blind to age, ethnicity and gender, and this is a solidly old-fashioned staging.
As a production it is packed with action and deft in its fight scenes, but remains rather flat, and perhaps unwilling to plumb this play's tragic depths.
But in going for speed and clarity of diction, Branagh has lost much of the emotional depth and reach of this great play.
This unwise tactic has been playing to diminishing returns for years now and fatally undermines his take on one of the most iconic roles in Shakespeare.
But too often it's a show in a rush, one that skates over the play's great theme of man's inhumanity to man.
Exhibiting neither frailty nor vulnerability, he robs us of any basis for sympathy.
This is less King Lear and more King Ken.
Confused in concept and clumsy in execution, it manages to be at once overblown and insubstantial.
He is captivating, at times entrancing.

This is the shortest playing of King Lear that I have seen. Though it doesn't explore its meaning (or find much of the humour that is also there), its brevity and its clear storyline could be a good introduction to the play.
Their characters and lines are cut, and they race through their speeches, skating gamely along the surface but never penetrating the depths beneath.
It feels like a trial run and that Branagh's Lear is still to come.
The show runs without an interval, and it feels like a visit to a booster-jab clinic. No one wants to be there but it's worth celebrating once you're clear of the building.
This is an attractively, if unevenly, packaged version 'King Lear'.
Branagh's vision is undeniably there, but the execution lacks directorial precision.
A fantastic take on a new facet of a timeless classic.

cn.t: Branagh's "King Lear" earns mostly positive reviews for its compelling staging and powerful moments, though some critics find the production uneven. Strong performances and simple yet effective design elevate this bleak, human take on Shakespeare's tragedy.
